author: ExtremePrivilege
body:
Extended Release, Delayed Release and Sustained Release are common questions asked by pharmacy students coming through on rotations. It's actually a lot more complicated than it sounds at face value. Some drugs are "extended release" due to their salt form, like Metoprolol tartrate versus succinate and it is mostly to do with absorption. Some drugs are extended release due to coatings or outer capsules that protect them from gastric acid but then promptly release in the duodenum (and partially the stomach). Aspirin, some iron products, things like Omeprazole. But some drugs get their ER, XL, DR, SR from their actual dosage form having unique pharmaceutic properties that slow the drug's release in the GI tract. These are highly varied. Some drugs slowly release through tiny pores in the coating. Some drugs are designed to have their "shell" remain intact all the way through to the feces (you can see them in the toilet!). Some drugs use diffusion, osmosis, or a controlled dissolution of the vehicle. Reservoir and Matrix systems often use polymer coatings that slowly dissolve allowing the drug through the membrane (reservoir) or matrices. Osmotic coatings (usually cellulose of some kind) have hard coatings with specific pores and numerous drug compartments. Some formulations even "swell" to release APIs.

I know this wasn't a direct answer to your question, but u/Zelman already gave you that. This is more of a broad overview of the pharmaceutics of oral drug delivery systems, how we achieve different rates of dissolution, and how one drug might have an IR, ER and XR formulation (bupropion, diltiazem, zolpidem) and that they're not interchangeable and sort of how that process works.

Concerta is probably my favorite one. VERY interesting mechanism of release.
